title: 19 September 2026
standfirst: Headline claims from one night of tracking. Each one carries the document it came from, the page it was read on, the date it was read, and the status it cannot be posted above.
runningOrder: Open with 04 (the silence) or 11 (the paddock); both land without context. Build through 05, 06, 12. Close on 10, which reframes everything before it. Hold 03 back unless the caveat can travel with it.

cards.title: the 66
cards.claim: Data centre load accounts for [[66 per cent]] of the growth in NSW end-use energy consumption from FY26 to FY35.
cards.note: Verbatim from the executive summary panel. It is 66% of growth in end-use consumption, not of consumption. The decade it is measured against also contains electrifying transport, heating and industry; everything else combined is the other third.

cards.title: the revision
cards.claim: In twelve months, Transgrid's forecast of data centre load growth to 2035 went up [[four times]].
cards.source: TRANSGRID · 2026 TAPR, AGAINST ITS OWN 2025 REPORT
cards.note: Quoted as "now forecast at 4x 2025 Transmission Annual Planning Report data centre forecasts". The same operator, one year apart. Any planning assumption formed from the 2025 report is wrong by a factor of four.

cards.title: the queue
cards.claim: NSW's grid operator has received data centre connection enquiries totalling [[20 gigawatts]], roughly twice the entire state's peak demand.
cards.note: Important. These are enquiries, not commitments. Transgrid states plainly that some are speculative or duplicated across networks, which is why Baringa was commissioned to de-duplicate. Never report this as approved or committed capacity. This is the card most likely to be attacked, and the caveat must travel with it.

cards.title: the silence
cards.claim: City of Moreton Bay has published [[16,519]] development applications since 2016. The word "data" appears in [[none]] of them.
cards.source: CITY OF MORETON BAY OPEN DATA · QUERIED 19·09·2026
cards.note: This project's own query. The index was verified working against controls (DWELLING 3,302, INDUSTR 402), but has not been independently checked. The council hosts Supernode, a data centre and battery campus reported at $2.5 to 3bn whose planning approval was announced by the Deputy Premier. The count is over application descriptions, not permit documents.

cards.title: the two vocabularies
cards.claim: One grid operator's annual report says "data centre" [[187 times]]. A decade of one council's planning applications says it [[zero]].
cards.source: TRANSGRID 2026 TAPR · CITY OF MORETON BAY OPEN DATA
cards.note: The comparison is this project's. The honest framing is that these are different kinds of document. The point is not that one is lazy; it is that the energy system has a word for these facilities and the planning system does not. Queensland consents them as "utility installation" or "high impact industry".

cards.title: capacity without consumption
cards.claim: A 113-page engineering report for Australia's largest proposed data centre states its grid connection, [[2,160 MVA]], and never once states how much electricity it will use.
cards.source: WESTERN DOWNS DIGITAL PARK · INFRASTRUCTURE SERVICES REPORT
cards.meta: WESTERN DOWNS REGIONAL COUNCIL REGISTER · RETRIEVED 19·09·2026
cards.note: SOURCED for the figure; UNVERIFIED for the absence, so the card sits at the lower of the two. No PUE, no WUE, no kWh, no MWh anywhere in 113 pages. A connection size is how big the pipe is, not how much flows through it, and with no efficiency figure stated, one cannot be derived from the other.

cards.title: the water that counts
cards.claim: The same report discloses [[16.5 kilolitres a day]] of operating water. It discloses twenty times that for construction.
cards.source: WESTERN DOWNS DIGITAL PARK · INFRASTRUCTURE SERVICES REPORT
cards.note: Construction demand is around 322 kL/day plus around 200 kL/day dust suppression, and 26.9 ML one-off per building to commission the closed loop. Both figures are real; the audit counts operating water only, and says so.

cards.title: the value of a hyperscaler
cards.claim: The capital investment value recorded for an Amazon data centre in Western Sydney is [[$14.7 million]].
cards.source: NSW EPLANNING ONLINEDA · AWS SYD52, SMEATON GRANGE
cards.note: Important. The figure is from the statutory feed and is almost certainly correct as the regulation defines it. The claim is not that anyone understated anything; it is that the statutory figure and what a hyperscaler actually spends are different measurements, and only one of them is recorded. Check what NSW CIV excludes before publishing.

cards.title: the uncountable pipeline
cards.claim: Of 94 Australian data centres tracked, [[one]] has both a disclosed value and a recorded approval date.
cards.note: This project's own coverage, and partly a statement about the tracker rather than the world. Six rows carry an investment figure, eight an approval date. Be explicit that this is harvesting coverage, not proof no record exists.

cards.title: approved before the question existed
cards.claim: Supernode's planning approval was announced in [[July 2022]]. ChatGPT launched that November.
cards.note: Primary source, ministerial statement, date on the document. The consent now underwriting a hyperscale AI campus was granted before the public conversation about AI infrastructure existed. Whatever conditions it carries were written for a different thing.

cards.title: the paddock
cards.claim: Street View, 2026. The site of a [[$3 billion]] data centre campus. The transmission towers on the horizon are the reason it is worth anything.
cards.source: BRENDALE, CITY OF MORETON BAY · GOOGLE STREET VIEW 2026
cards.note: SOURCED for the value. Google's imagery, reproduced with source and date named; consider a photograph taken on the public road if this goes to print. The strongest image of the night and the whole siting argument in one frame. Land, water, energy is the one layer Australia holds, and the energy part is allocated by a contract that appears in no planning record.
cards.imageAlt: Google Street View of an empty grassed paddock at Brendale in the City of Moreton Bay, with high-voltage transmission towers running along the horizon.

cards.title: the shape, not the size
cards.claim: NSW minimum demand stops falling in [[2029]] and turns back up, because of data centre load.
cards.note: This is the subtle one and possibly the most important. These facilities run flat, day and night. They are not a bigger version of existing demand; they are a different kind of load, and they change the hardest problem in a solar-heavy grid.

cards.title: the forecast that wasn't
cards.claim: In 2025 Queensland's transmission planner reported [["limited interest from data centre proponents"]] and left them out of its load forecast entirely.
cards.note: Verbatim. The full sentence is "with minimal enquiries or developments progressing beyond preliminary stages", and the conclusion is "Powerlink has not included specific data centre projects into the current load forecast." This is the network planner for the state that now hosts both Supernode and the largest data centre proposed in Australia.

cards.title: off by two orders of magnitude
cards.claim: AEMO projected [[90 GWh]] a year of data centre consumption for all of Queensland. One proposed site is around a hundred times that.
cards.source: AEMO 2025 INPUTS, ASSUMPTIONS AND SCENARIOS · VIA POWERLINK 2025 TAPR
cards.meta: WESTERN DOWNS DIGITAL PARK · DA LODGED 17·08·2026
cards.note: SOURCED for the 90 GWh; the comparison is this project's arithmetic, so the card sits at the lower of the two. State the assumptions. Western Downs is 1,440 MW of IT load (4 × 360 MW). At 8,760 hours and a 70% load factor that is around 8,800 GWh a year, about 98× the 90 GWh figure. Load factor is an assumption, not a disclosure; the record states no consumption figure at all, which is card 06. Say so.

cards.title: the forecast still in force
cards.claim: Queensland's current published transmission forecast contains [[no data centre projects]]. Its data is current as at September 2025.
cards.source: POWERLINK · 2025 TAPR §2.3.7, STILL THE CURRENT EDITION
cards.note: SOURCED for the quote; UNVERIFIED that no 2026 edition exists, which rests on a search rather than on a statement from Powerlink. Be fair: annual reports are annual, and this is not a claim that Powerlink is unaware. They almost certainly hold current enquiry data they have not published. The claim is about the public record: the forecast a citizen or a council can read today excludes a facility lodged in August 2026 at roughly a hundred times the statewide projection. Ask Powerlink before publishing.

cards.title: the queue doubled
cards.claim: In March 2026 NSW's grid operator reported [[10 GW]] of data centre connection enquiries. By its annual report later that year: [[20 GW]].
cards.note: Both figures verbatim, both dated. These are the same measure at two points in time, not a discrepancy. The March submission also says around 6 GW of that was "progressing at pace" to a formal application, which is the honest answer to how much of the 20 GW is real, and Transgrid compares that 6 GW to building a Renewable Energy Zone the size of Central-West Orana.

cards.title: the size that disappears
cards.claim: Data centres connecting to NSW transmission range from [[250 MW to over 1,200 MW]], averaging 650 MW. Smaller ones connect to the distribution network instead.
cards.note: This is the threshold at which a facility stops being visible to the network that plans and prices for households. Above it, a data centre connects straight to transmission, which is what both Queensland sites do, and why Victoria's planner separately counts "small distribution connected data centres".
